Insurance Thought Leadership · hace 2 días · 1 min General

Let’s get real about non-weather water loss reduction with IoT

LeakBot's 65,000 years of US underwriting data proves actuarially relevant loss mitigation: mature programs cut non-weather mains-related water claims ~60%, and the $5/month all-in model delivers positive ROI across market segments. Proving a sensor prevented a claim runs into three structural problems: there’s no dated invoice for a loss that never happened, early results are skewed by anti-selection bias and poor test design, and the real benefit only emerges once a program has matured well beyond its first few months. Most IoT loss-prevention studies don’t survive actuarial scrutiny — underpowered samples, uncorrected selection bias, and hidden program costs have left carriers unable to trust the ROI case for smart-home safety programs, or to justify scaling one past a pilot.

Car Crashes Spike on New Album Release Days: Study

A newly released study found that car crashes spiked on major music album release days than on the 10 days before and after, according to “Smartphones, Online Music Streaming, and Traffic Fatalities,” published on the JAMA Open Network. Excess fatalities occurring on album release days were higher among drivers who were younger and male and among crashes where a single occupant was involved, the weather was clear, alcohol was not involved, and vehicles were manufactured with infotainment systems. The research, the result of collaboration among researchers from the Department of Health Care Policy, Harvard Medical School, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Massachusetts General Hospital, and the National Bureau of Economic Research, found that daily music streaming volumes rose on dates of major album releases compared with the 10 days before and after releases, from 86.1 million to 123.3 million, an increase of 43%.

Severe weather losses in Manitoba and Saskatchewan – neighbouring provinces located in Western and Central Canada – have climbed above $840 million, according to the latest estimate from Catastrophe Indices and Quantification Inc. Since 2021, Manitoba and Saskatchewan have experienced 30 catastrophic weather events resulting in over $2.5 billion in insured losses. So far in 2026, five of Canada’s 11 catastrophic weather events have affected Manitoba and Saskatchewan, including a dust storm with damaging winds that caused $40 million in insured losses.
